transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess I'm here because things have just been... really intense lately, and my schedule just completely spiraled out of control. I mean, I just moved into this new apartment, which was a whole ordeal on its own, you know? There were just boxes everywhere, and I was barely settling in—literally just trying to figure out where I packed my silverware and getting my home monitors set up. 

But then, almost out of nowhere, I just shifted gears completely. I went from just trying to unpack my life to suddenly... well, I started saying yes to all these mentoring sessions for junior designers, which I usually never have the bandwidth for. And then I took on all these extra client prototypes at work. I'm a digital interface designer, so building out interactive prototypes takes a massive amount of focus and time, but I just kept volunteering for them, thinking, 'Oh, I can definitely handle this.' 

And then, on top of all that, I decided I needed to completely redesign my entire professional portfolio from scratch. It was like... I don't know, it felt exactly like I had to fix my entire life and career in one single sprint, you know? Like Agile methodology but applied to my actual existence. I just kept adding and adding to my plate, and I couldn't seem to just sit still in my new place, and honestly it just got so overwhelming that I realized something was probably off.
During this period, were you sleeping much less than usual and still feeling rested?

Oh, completely. It was actually bizarre. Normally, if I do not get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just a total zombie. I can barely look at a monitor, let alone align pixels or build out complex user journeys. But during this whole... whatever it was, this massive burst of energy, I was barely sleeping at all. 

For several nights in a row, I think I slept maybe three, possibly four hours max. I would finally force myself into bed at like two in the morning because I knew I logically needed to sleep, but then my eyes would just pop open at five or five-thirty. And the weirdest part was that I was not tired. Not even a little bit. I woke up completely convinced that I was totally fine, like my body had just magically adapted to not needing rest anymore. 

I remember lying there in the dark, looking at the ceiling in my new bedroom, which still did not even have curtains yet, just those cheap temporary paper blinds I grabbed from the hardware store, and I just thought, well, I am awake, I have all this extra time, I should really use it to get ahead. So I would just get right back up, make coffee, open up my laptop, and dive straight back into my portfolio wireframes or those extra client prototypes before the sun was even up. It just felt like a superpower at the time, like I had unlocked this secret extra part of the day that nobody else had access to, and I just could not stop myself from using every single second of it, even though looking back it was probably way too much.
During that high-energy period, did you feel unusually confident or powerful compared with your normal self?

Um... confident? Or powerful? No, not really. I mean, I definitely felt like I could get a massive amount of work done, like I mentioned with all those extra client prototypes and the mentoring sessions, but it wasn't like I thought I was suddenly the absolute best designer in the world or anything like that. 

Actually, in my field—interface design—things just change so incredibly fast. There's always a new tool, or a new Figma update, or new web accessibility standards you have to memorize, so I usually have a pretty healthy amount of... I guess you could call it imposter syndrome? Or at least just realism about my skills. And that didn't really go away. Even when I was pulling those crazy hours and completely redoing my entire portfolio from scratch in the middle of the night, I was still obsessing over every little detail, like whether my drop shadows were too heavy or if my grid system was fundamentally flawed. 

I didn't feel like a superhero in terms of my actual talent, if that makes sense? I just felt like an absolute machine in terms of my output. I was just churning and churning through the work, pixel-pushing at lightning speed. But confident? Powerful? No, honestly, I was probably just as insecure about my actual design choices as I always am. Maybe even more so, honestly, because I was moving so fast and not taking the time to set up review sessions to get proper feedback from the senior art directors like I normally would. I just felt... incredibly busy. Really, really driven to just keep producing and checking things off a list, but definitely not like I was suddenly invincible or on top of the world.
During that high-energy period, were you talking much more than usual?

Um, talking more? No, I don't think so. I mean, honestly, I was so laser-focused on my screens that I was probably talking *less* to actual human beings. 

I was working from home in the new apartment, right? So it was just me, the boxes I hadn't unpacked yet, and my dual-monitor setup. When you're in the zone like that, especially when you're building out these really intricate interactive components—like, I was working on this one prototype for a client where every single button state had to have a custom micro-animation, which is incredibly tedious but looks amazing when it's done—you just don't have time to chat. You can't break your concentration. 

Even with the mentoring sessions I took on, those were mostly me just reviewing their Figma files and leaving comments, or doing quick screen shares where I was just sort of rapidly pointing out alignment issues or explaining why their typography hierarchy was confusing. It wasn't like I was rambling or dominating a conversation at a dinner party or anything. 

Actually, my mom called me right in the middle of that week, right when I was knee-deep in redesigning the landing page for my portfolio, and I remember I practically rushed her off the phone. She just wanted to know if I had found my winter coats in the move, and I was just like, "Mom, I can't, I have to finish this sprint, I'll call you later." And I didn't even call her back for like three days because I was just so locked into the work. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I was more talkative. If anything, I was probably a lot shorter with people because I felt like any conversation that wasn't directly about the work I was doing was just slowing me down and getting in the way of everything I needed to accomplish. I just wanted everyone to leave me alone so I could keep producing.
During that high-energy period, did it cause serious problems in your life or work?

Um... well, yes. I mean, at the time I thought I was absolutely crushing it, but... yeah, it actually did cause some pretty significant issues. 

Especially at work. Because I was so hyper-focused on all those extra little things I mentioned, like the custom micro-animations and completely redoing my entire portfolio from scratch, I actually completely lost track of my actual, real-world obligations. Like, I had this major design review scheduled with the senior art director and the project managers for one of our biggest client accounts. It had been on the calendar for weeks. And I just... completely blew right past it. I was so deep in my own little bubble, just churning out screens and thinking I was being so productive, that I totally ignored my Slack notifications, my calendar alerts, my emails, everything. By the time I finally snapped out of it and looked at the clock, I was like three hours late to a very important sync, and they had to scramble to cover for me. It was incredibly unprofessional. 

And then, on top of that, my personal life has kind of been a disaster because of it. Like I mentioned with my mom earlier? How I just rushed her off the phone when she asked about my winter coats? Well, I've basically been doing that to everyone. I have been completely avoiding my friends, my family... just dodging calls and leaving text messages on read for days, sometimes weeks. 

And it's not even because I'm too busy to reply anymore, it's just... I feel so incredibly embarrassed. When I look back at how I was acting, or when I try to explain myself to them, I just sound so scattered. Like I'm completely all over the place, dropping the ball on important meetings, ignoring people who care about me, just being totally unreliable. I've always prided myself on being the organized one—I mean, my literal job is organizing complex information so it makes sense to users—so knowing that everyone around me, from my boss to my mother, is seeing me act this erratic and undependable... I just can't face them. I really can't. I'd honestly rather just hide out here in my half-unpacked apartment with my paper blinds than have to look anyone in the eye and explain why I've been such a mess lately.
Have you ever had a period of at least a couple of weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Um... yes. Definitely. That's actually... that's kind of where I'm at right now, honestly. It's been like this for, I don't know, a good three or four weeks at this point? It's just this constant, overwhelming feeling. 

Lately, I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling in my chest. It's like... it's like a physical weight, right in the center of my ribs. And it doesn't matter what time I wake up, or how much sleep I got, or what the weather is like outside. It's just there. The second I open my eyes, before I even remember what day it is or what I'm supposed to be doing, that heaviness is just sitting there waiting for me. 

And the weirdest part is that it happens even when there's absolutely no reason for it. Like, I'll be sitting in my apartment, and it's perfectly quiet, right? The paper blinds are drawn, I don't have any immediate deadlines because I've sort of pushed everything off, and nothing actively bad is happening in that exact moment. But I just feel so incredibly sad. I'll walk into the kitchen to get a glass of water, and I'll see a coffee mug sitting in the sink—just a regular, dirty coffee mug that I left there the day before—and I feel like I could just break down and cry over it. Just start sobbing over a mug. 

It makes no sense. It's not like the mug is a symbol of my failures or anything, it's just... the sadness is so close to the surface that literally anything can trigger it. It's exhausting. I spend the entire day just trying to hold back tears over the stupidest things. I can't even look at my Figma files right now because just the thought of trying to pick a color palette or align a button makes me feel like crying. It's just this pervasive, dark cloud that follows me from the bed to the couch and back to the bed again, day in and day out.
About that high-energy period, did it last for at least 7 days?

Seven days? Oh, um, it was definitely longer than that. I mean, if I really sit and look at the calendar and try to piece the timeline together... this whole intense up-and-down pattern has been going on since I moved into the apartment about a month ago. 

I remember because I signed the lease right at the end of the previous month, and I had this weird overlap week where I was just ferrying fragile things over in my car—like my dual monitors and my good ergonomic chair—before the actual movers came with the heavy furniture. And right from the jump, almost as soon as I got the keys, it was just this absolute rollercoaster. 

I initially chalked it up to just the adrenaline of the move, you know? Because moving is always so chaotic and it totally wrecks your normal routine, so I thought I was just riding that wave of nervous energy. But that wired, obsessive energy just kept going and going, way past a week. I was just locked in, totally losing track of time, completely ignoring the boxes piling up around me. And then, of course, it eventually flipped into this awful, heavy gray feeling I'm dealing with now. 

So, yeah, it hasn't just been a few days or a week. This entire exhausting cycle, the extreme highs and now this low, has basically been dictating my life for a solid month now.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a distinct period of abnormally increased energy and goal-directed activity lasting longer than 7 days, with markedly decreased need for sleep and significant functional impairment, consistent with a manic episode despite limited classic grandiosity or pressured speech. This was followed by a current depressive episode lasting 3–4 weeks with pervasive depressed mood and tearfulness. The longitudinal pattern supports bipolar affective disorder, current episode mild or moderate depression.
